Space of definitions. Across the papers, the prevailing usage treats code generation as producing executable, functional, or functionally correct source code from a natural language description, prompt, docstring, or other specification. Success is usually framed by syntactic validity plus whether the generated code works, often by passing unit, visible, or hidden tests, though some papers instead emphasize complete, compilable solutions or code that reproduces a target artifact. A smaller line of work broadens the input beyond plain text to multimodal prompts, chart images, code skeletons, input-output examples, or repository context. One paper explicitly describes it as the task of synthesizing code from natural language (SWE-bench Multimodal: Do AI Systems Generalize to Visual Software Domains?).

Variants. Papers use the label for many variants. Common ones stay close to function- or program-level synthesis, including function completion, whole-function and repo-level generation, class-level generation, standalone function implementation, and sequential edit generation. Another cluster covers multimodal or structured targets, such as chart-to-code generation, visual program generation, mockup-to-code, slide code generation, and text-to-ES or ORM query generation. Other papers narrow it to particular languages or domains, including Python and multilingual coding, Verilog or other HDL tasks, interactive Bash coding, backend application generation, EDA and visualization code, game code, Prolog programs, and policy-to-code translation. In repository settings, one paper defines the task as generating the target function that passes all relevant test cases (Can Language Models Replace Programmers for Coding? REPOCOD Says `Not Yet').

Space of elicitation and scores. Code generation is measured by 32 instruments. The most recurrent are HumanEval, MBPP, APPS, LiveCodeBench, and EvalPlus, which papers use for function-level Python tasks, broader programming problems, and test-augmented evaluation. Most linked instruments are benchmark datasets, though papers also mention execution-based evaluation and an LLM-as-a-judge setup.

What it is taken as evidence of. Across 17 linked constructs, a direct measurement-style use treats code generation as evidence of coding ability, and papers also frequently tie it to reasoning. On reasoning, papers do not use a single direction: some report code generation is related to reasoning, others claim reasoning causes code generation, and another line claims code generation causes reasoning. Smaller lines of work connect it to planning, algorithmic reasoning, and expressive power. Overall, papers do not converge on one construct that code generation reflects.

characterization_sections.label: Space of definitions.
characterization_sections.text: Across the papers, the prevailing usage treats code generation as producing executable, functional, or functionally correct source code from a natural language description, prompt, docstring, or other specification. Success is usually framed by syntactic validity plus whether the generated code works, often by passing unit, visible, or hidden tests, though some papers instead emphasize complete, compilable solutions or code that reproduces a target artifact. A smaller line of work broadens the input beyond plain text to multimodal prompts, chart images, code skeletons, input-output examples, or repository context. One paper explicitly describes it as the task of synthesizing code from natural language (SWE-bench Multimodal: Do AI Systems Generalize to Visual Software Domains?).

characterization_sections.label: Variants.
characterization_sections.text: Papers use the label for many variants. Common ones stay close to function- or program-level synthesis, including function completion, whole-function and repo-level generation, class-level generation, standalone function implementation, and sequential edit generation. Another cluster covers multimodal or structured targets, such as chart-to-code generation, visual program generation, mockup-to-code, slide code generation, and text-to-ES or ORM query generation. Other papers narrow it to particular languages or domains, including Python and multilingual coding, Verilog or other HDL tasks, interactive Bash coding, backend application generation, EDA and visualization code, game code, Prolog programs, and policy-to-code translation. In repository settings, one paper defines the task as generating the target function that passes all relevant test cases (Can Language Models Replace Programmers for Coding? REPOCOD Says `Not Yet').

characterization_sections.label: Space of elicitation and scores.
characterization_sections.text: Code generation is measured by 32 instruments. The most recurrent are HumanEval, MBPP, APPS, LiveCodeBench, and EvalPlus, which papers use for function-level Python tasks, broader programming problems, and test-augmented evaluation. Most linked instruments are benchmark datasets, though papers also mention execution-based evaluation and an LLM-as-a-judge setup.

characterization_sections.label: What it is taken as evidence of.
characterization_sections.text: Across 17 linked constructs, a direct measurement-style use treats code generation as evidence of coding ability, and papers also frequently tie it to reasoning. On reasoning, papers do not use a single direction: some report code generation is related to reasoning, others claim reasoning causes code generation, and another line claims code generation causes reasoning. Smaller lines of work connect it to planning, algorithmic reasoning, and expressive power. Overall, papers do not converge on one construct that code generation reflects.
